# AI Build Kit

> AI Build Kit helps people without a software background and small teams plan, build and run tools with an AI coding agent, without requiring them to read code. It installs eleven skills: six commands the person types and five background skills the commands call.

The person explains what should happen, tries the result and decides on risk.
The kit suits internal tools with a manual fallback.

Works with: Claude Code is tested. Codex is expected to work. Cursor, Gemini CLI,
GitHub Copilot and other agents are experimental. The Compatibility page gives
the grades and known limits. An agent must read and edit files, run shell
commands and use Git.

Install (shared installer): `npx skills add gwpicard/ai-build-kit`
Install (Claude Code terminal app only): `claude plugin marketplace add gwpicard/ai-build-kit`
then `claude plugin install ai-build-kit@ai-build-kit --scope local`
Use one route per project. Ask the agent to run the setup-ai-build-kit skill;
on the Claude plugin route, type `/ai-build-kit:setup-ai-build-kit`.
Compatibility also explains manual installation and Agent Plugins.

Commands:

- `/setup-ai-build-kit` interviews the person and prepares the project once.
- `/shape` turns an idea or a reproduced fault into a ready piece, one task with a checkable result.
- `/implement` builds a ready piece, shows the result and merges on the person's yes. With several ready, it shows what can be built together and asks which to take.
- `/setup-hosting` sets up how the tool runs live and checks or changes that later.
- `/maintain` makes the records true again, reads the live copy and reports gaps, and runs upkeep when due. It also prepares handovers and switches a tool off.
- `/what-now` says where the project stands and what to do next.

Records: `masterplan.md` describes the tool now, GitHub issues hold work still to
do, and `CHANGELOG.md` records what happened. A checkpoint is a saved snapshot.
Setup opens issues in a named repository the person owns, with a warning if
public. Code stays local until the first piece that uploads it asks permission.
Every merge needs the person's yes.

Going live: two recipes pair tools for building a web app with a place to run
it. The README names them and links their plan terms and trial records. Other
stacks get a general checklist with fewer checks. Once live, each approved merge
puts the change in front of users. Rollback means returning to an earlier live
version; launch checks confirm an earlier build exists without trying one.

Safety: the build path decides how much checking a project needs. A sensitive
area gets a risk notice and the person decides whether to carry on, with their
acceptance recorded. A run left on its own stops at a sensitive area. Secrets
stay out of files Git tracks. Agent approval settings vary; see Compatibility.

Teams: one person or a small team, using pull requests. The kit does not suit
large teams or many agents building at once. It adds steps; a hosted builder is
faster for a quick throwaway demo.

Cost and limits: the kit is free under the MIT licence, without warranty. Agent
subscriptions and hosting have their own prices. Risk notices miss things and
passing checks only cover what somebody thought to check. The kit cannot
replace a professional developer or provide legal, medical, financial or
security advice.
